newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Asian gas oil set to breach record levels.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Asian gas oil set to breach record levels.

text.p: Singapore diesel prices were quoted at a five-year high on renewed Iraq tension and were poised to breach post-Gulf War record levels as the market enters a period of peak demand, industry sources said on Friday. The high market prices could feed into service stations and push up prices at the pump.
The traders said benchmark spot prices for diesel, or gas oil, were quoted at $28.60 per barrel in Singapore on Thursday, 30 cents above its previous peak in February this year.

They said the market was poised to trade at current high levels, citing low stocks in the West, latent Chinese demand, reduced exports from the Middle East, traders buying to fill Indian orders and strong winter demand.
China, the region's largest diesel importer, had not bought much spot product since the early September, they said. It imports between 600,000 to 800,000 tonnes a month.
China, which uses diesel primarily for power generation, had chosen to stay out of the spot market when prices spiked up following the U.S. first missile attack on Iraq on September 3.
But low stocks forced China to buy one cargo on Thursday at $213-214 on a cost-and-freight basis, about $7 per tonne more that its previous purchase.
Stronger prices were also supported by low heating oil stocks in the West and North Asia, a source at one oil major said.
In the United States, October heating oil on the NYMEX rose to 68.20 cents per gallon, its highest price since November of 1991 and close to its post-Gulf war high of 72.25 cents.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) said on Wednesday distillate stocks, which include diesel, were about 20 million barrels below normal for this time of the year.
The EIA blamed a large part of this to low heating oil stocks on the U.S. East Coast, which are at half of last year's level.
Heating oil stocks on the East Coast stood at 21.4 million barrels compared with 41.4 million barrels a year ago.

The strength of diesel prices was also seen in Europe, where September diesel futures on the International Petroleum Exchange were traded at a five-year of $223 per tonne, just off its post-Gulf War high of $226.50.
Strong European prices had led to an unusual export from the Middle East to East Africa and the Mediterranean -- two areas not normally supplied from the Middle East.
Middle East diesel exports to East Asia and India were sharply reduced as a result.
Traders with term and spot committments to India, especially for deliveries to the east coast, were forced to cover their shortfall in supplies from Singapore, traders said.
Refiners are also paying more for diesel-rich crudes, such as Malaysia's Tapis.
One refinery source said they were paying about $1.50 per barrel more for Tapis type crudes over the region's benchmark Dubai crude.
